summary: A chronicle-based area-control game where a persistent world evolves session to session, with players negotiating, warring, and betraying each other to seize or hold power over an ancient land. Every playthrough writes a bit of history that shapes the setup and stakes of the next.
praised: genuinely emergent, novel-feeling narrative across sessions
deep asymmetric strategy and meaningful long-term consequences
criticised: steep, unusual rulebook that's hard to onboard new players into
best experienced with a stable group playing repeatedly, which not everyone has
can feel chaotic or punishing in early plays before the world settles

interaction.kind: direct area-majority conflict, dice-based attacks, and open negotiation/betrayal
interaction.detail: Players fight over the same regions and Chancellor's favor with dice combat, actively deny each other cards and sites, and negotiate deals or betrayals that shape who wins outright. The legacy layer means today's conflicts and alliances change the shared world state for every future game, so almost nothing here is played in isolation.

scoring.how_you_win: The reigning Chancellor wins by satisfying whatever Oath the previous game set (usually majority control of a suit's favor or sites); an Exile instead wins by secretly completing their Vision card and revealing it to depose the Chancellor.
scoring.score_note: won via one of several non-score conditions

theme.said: praised for its Chronicle system 'writing real history', though the underlying area-majority/combat engine is often noted as similar to other Wehrle/Root-style games underneath
theme.why: the World Deck's Records, Relics, and shifting Vision (which literally rewrites next game's win condition based on what happened this game) exist only because the game is trying to model how history and legend accumulate across reigns

style.why: A euro-ish area-influence economy is wrapped in a legacy narrative with real conflict, dice, and take-that that can swing the game hard.
